humanities_role_explanation: Parole hearing transcripts (legal-institutional spoken discourse) supply the material; the competence tested is general LLM style imitation/impersonation via prompting, measured with linguistic features. It is not a test of disciplinary humanities competence, though it is a linguistic analysis study.
benchmark_modalities_explanation: Text only: transcripts of parole hearings are input, and models generate spoken-style decision statements as text.
analytical_tasks_explanation: Models generate parole decision statements impersonating a specific presiding commissioner, with or without a speaker-specific 'rhetorical fingerprint' in the prompt. Output is analysed via stylistic features (sentence complexity, MTLD lexical diversity, discourse markers, nominalizations, modals, pronouns, jargon) expressed as z-scores against original statements.

general_purpose_benchmark.note: Single-task, single-domain study (California parole hearing decision statements); no general benchmark is introduced.

quantitative_metrics.note: Per-feature z-scores of linguistic features, MTLD, relative frequencies.

summary: The paper distills speaker-specific rhetorical fingerprints from presiding commissioners' parole decision statements and uses them to enhance prompts for LLM impersonation. Comparing against a primed-by-corpus prompt, it finds LLMs only partly approximate features and retain their own model-specific fingerprint.
key_findings: All three LLMs deviate strongly in lexical diversity and sentence complexity (z-scores 5.76 to 40.20 and 16.52 to 34.91) regardless of prompt; nominalizations are overused, discourse markers and first-person plural are underused; fingerprint prompts bring small adjustments only; GPT-4o and GPT-4.1 have near-identical shapes, DeepSeek barely changes between conditions.
evaluation_unit: parole hearing transcript (one generated decision statement per transcript per model and condition)
facets_explanation: There are no reference answers in the usual sense: the original commissioner statements from CDCR transcripts serve as the stylistic baseline, with features computed automatically (spaCy, MTLD, PDTB markers, hand-curated wordlists). The paper does not describe an answer key, annotators or any treatment of disagreement.
results_explanation: The paper compares the fingerprint prompt against the primed-by-corpus prompt on z-scores of features (Table 1), e.g. DeepSeek nominalization z-score 'was 6.47 for primed-by-corpus and 9.1 for fingerprint condition'. No numeric gap in points is given, so reported_format_gap_points is null, and no single headline score exists because results are per-feature z-scores.

humanities_role.quote: we explore the limits of popular LLMs in impersonating content in a high-stakes legal setting, namely for the generation of the decision statement in parole suitability hearings

dataset_size.quote: PSH v1.0, comprises 100 parole hearing transcripts that we requested from the California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation

evaluation_set_size.quote: we select two female and two male presiding commissioners with 25 transcripts per commissioner

primary_evaluation_setting.quote: The three state-of-the-art models, namely GPT-4o, GPT-4.1 and DeepSeek R1, were accessed and prompted via their respective API

reported_format_gap.quote: z-score was 6.47 for primed-by-corpus and 9.1 for fingerprint condition

reported_format_gap_kind.quote: we mirror the fingerprint prompt with a simplified version of the user prompt, including only the general information about parole hearings
